content.text: Chapter 3, “Motion in a Plane,” extends the description of motion from one dimension to two dimensions (a plane) and three dimensions (space). In one dimension, direction can be represented with plus and minus signs because only two directions are possible. In a plane or in space, displacement, velocity and acceleration require vectors. The chapter introduces vector operations, resolution into components, motion with constant acceleration, projectile motion and uniform circular motion. The equations developed for a plane can be extended to three dimensions.

A scalar quantity has magnitude only and is specified by a number and an appropriate unit. Examples include distance, mass, temperature, time, volume, density and speed. Scalars combine according to ordinary algebra, with addition or subtraction meaningful for quantities with the same units. A vector has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle or parallelogram law of addition. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. A vector may be written in boldface or with an arrow; its magnitude is denoted by vertical bars, such as |A|. In general, the magnitude of displacement is less than or equal to path length.

Choose an origin O to describe an object’s position in a plane. If the object is at P, its position vector is r = OP. If it moves from P to P′, the displacement vector is PP′ = r′ − r. Displacement is the straight vector joining the initial and final positions and does not depend on the actual path. Different paths between the same endpoints therefore have the same displacement, while their path lengths may differ. The path length equals the magnitude of displacement only when the direction does not change.

Two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same magnitude and direction. In this chapter vectors are treated as free vectors: shifting a vector parallel to itself does not change it. In physical applications where location or line of application matters, vectors may instead be localised vectors. Equal vectors need not occupy the same position in a diagram.

content.text: Multiplying vector A by a real number λ produces vector λA. Its magnitude is |λ| times the magnitude of A. If λ is positive, the direction remains the same; if λ is negative, the direction reverses; if λ = 0, the result is the zero vector. The vector −A has the same magnitude as A but opposite direction, and A + (−A) = 0. A null vector has zero magnitude and no specified direction. The source lists properties A + 0 = A, λ0 = 0 and 0A = 0.

content.text: Vector addition can be performed using the head-to-tail (triangle) method or the parallelogram method. For head-to-tail addition, place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the second. For the parallelogram method, place both tails at a common origin and draw the parallelogram; the diagonal from the common tail is the resultant. Vector addition is commutative, A + B = B + A, and associative, (A + B) + C = A + (B + C). Graphical methods aid visualisation but can have limited accuracy.

Subtracting vector B from vector A is defined as adding the negative of B: A − B = A + (−B). Reverse B’s direction to obtain −B, then add it to A using the triangle or parallelogram method. The resultant runs from the tail of A to the head of −B when arranged head-to-tail.

Problem: Rain falls vertically at 35 m s⁻¹. Wind then blows from east to west at 12 m s⁻¹. Determine how a boy should hold his umbrella. The source combines the rain-velocity vector and wind-velocity vector. Their resultant magnitude is R = √(35² + 12²) = 37 m s⁻¹. The angle θ the resultant makes with the vertical satisfies tan θ = 12/35 = 0.343, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.343) ≈ 19°. The book concludes that the umbrella should be held in the vertical plane at about 19° with the vertical towards the east.

A vector A in a plane can be expressed as a sum of scalar multiples of two non-collinear vectors a and b: A = λa + μb, where λ and μ are real numbers. Geometrically, draw through the tail of A a line parallel to a and through its head a line parallel to b; the resulting parallelogram gives the two component vectors. In rectangular coordinates, resolve A into x- and y-components using unit vectors i and j. The components are Ax and Ay, so A = Ax i + Ay j. If θ is the angle measured from the positive x-axis, Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ; A = √(Ax² + Ay²), tan θ = Ay/Ax (with quadrant considered).

A unit vector has magnitude one and points in a specified direction. The unit vectors i, j and k point along the x-, y- and z-axes of a right-handed coordinate system. A vector in three dimensions may be expressed as A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k. Its components are signed scalar values along the coordinate axes. For a vector in the x-y plane, A = Ax i + Ay j, with Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ when θ is measured from the positive x-axis.
equations: A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k

content.text: Graphical addition can be inaccurate or tedious. Analytical addition combines corresponding components. If A = Ax i + Ay j and B = Bx i + By j, then R = A + B = (Ax + Bx)i + (Ay + By)j. For three-dimensional vectors, add the x-, y- and z-components separately. Subtraction is performed by subtracting corresponding components. The direction and magnitude of the resultant follow from its components.

The source derives the magnitude and direction of the resultant R of vectors A and B that make an angle θ. Using the parallelogram construction and right-triangle geometry, the resultant magnitude follows the cosine law. The direction angle α relative to A is obtained from the sine relation or tangent relation shown below. The example is a derivation in terms of A, B and θ rather than a numerical substitution.
equations: tan α = (B sin θ)/(A + B cos θ)

content.text: Problem: A motorboat moves north at 25 km/h while the water current is 10 km/h at 60° east of south. Find the resultant velocity. The source uses vector addition and the cosine law. The angle between the northward boat velocity and the current direction is 120°. The resultant magnitude is √(25² + 10² + 2×25×10 cos 120°) ≈ 21.8 km/h (reported approximately 22 km/h). Using the sine rule, sin φ = (10 sin 120°)/21.8 ≈ 0.397, giving φ ≈ 23.4° in the source’s diagram convention.

For an object at coordinates (x,y), the position vector is r = x i + y j. Between positions r and r′, displacement is Δr = r′ − r = (x′ − x)i + (y′ − y)j = Δx i + Δy j. Average velocity over time interval Δt is v_avg = Δr/Δt. Instantaneous velocity is the limit as Δt approaches zero, v = dr/dt. Its components are vx = dx/dt and vy = dy/dt. The instantaneous velocity vector is tangent to the trajectory and points in the direction of motion.
equations: Δr = r′ − r = Δx i + Δy j

content.text: If velocity changes from v to v′ during time Δt, average acceleration is a_avg = Δv/Δt = (v′ − v)/Δt. Instantaneous acceleration is a = lim(Δt→0)(Δv/Δt) = dv/dt. In component notation, a = ax i + ay j + az k, with ax = dvx/dt, ay = dvy/dt and az = dvz/dt. Velocity and acceleration need not point in the same direction. In curvilinear motion, the direction of the velocity changes as the object follows the path.
equations: ax = dvx/dt; ay = dvy/dt; az = dvz/dt

content.text: Problem: The position of a particle is r = 3.0t i + 2.0t² j + 5.0 k (metres, with coefficients carrying appropriate units). Differentiate position with respect to time to obtain v(t) = 3.0 i + 4.0t j. Differentiate again to obtain a(t) = 4.0 j, or 4.0 m s⁻² in the y-direction. At t = 1.0 s, v = 3.0 i + 4.0 j m s⁻¹, with magnitude √(3² + 4²) = 5.0 m s⁻¹. The direction is determined from the component ratio; the source’s printed angle expression is not reliably captured in the extracted text.

content.text: For constant acceleration a, velocity at time t is v = v₀ + at. The displacement from initial position r₀ is r − r₀ = v₀t + ½at², hence r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at². In components, x = x₀ + v₀x t + ½ax t² and y = y₀ + v₀y t + ½ay t²; vx = v₀x + ax t and vy = v₀y + ay t. These equations follow by applying the one-dimensional constant-acceleration relations independently along perpendicular axes. The vector equations do not depend on a particular choice of axes.
equations: x = x₀ + v₀x t + ½ax t²
y = y₀ + v₀y t + ½ay t²

content.text: The source example gives a particle starting at the origin in the x-y plane with an initial velocity and a constant acceleration, then asks for position and speed at a specified time/coordinate. The readable solution uses component equations, obtains x(t) = 5.0t + 1.5t² and y(t) = 1.0t², and sets x = 84 m to find t = 6 s. Then y = 36.0 m. Differentiating position gives v = (5.0 + 3.0t)i + 2.0t j; at t = 6 s, v = 23.0i + 12.0j m s⁻¹ and speed √(23² + 12²) ≈ 26 m s⁻¹. content.text: A projectile is an object in flight after being projected. The chapter analyses ideal projectile motion under gravity, neglecting air resistance. Choose x horizontal and y vertically upward, with initial speed v₀ at angle θ₀ above the x-axis and initial position at the origin. Horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is −g. The horizontal and vertical motions can be treated independently: horizontal velocity remains constant while vertical velocity changes due to gravity.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Projectile motion: assumptions and component equations

content.text: Eliminating time from the projectile component equations gives a parabolic trajectory. For launch and landing at the same vertical level, the time to maximum height is tₘ = v₀ sin θ₀/g, the maximum height is hₘ = v₀² sin²θ₀/(2g), and the horizontal range is R = v₀² sin(2θ₀)/g. These results assume constant gravitational acceleration, no air resistance, and equal initial and final heights for the range formula. The trajectory equation is y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/[2(v₀ cos θ₀)²].
equations: y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/[2(v₀ cos θ₀)²]

content.text: The chapter credits Galileo Galilei with recognising that projectile motion can be understood as the superposition of uniform horizontal motion and vertically accelerated motion due to gravity. The historical discussion refers to Galileo’s work and the book “Two New Sciences” (1638). Under the ideal assumptions, combining constant horizontal velocity with vertical acceleration produces a parabolic path.

This example discusses Galileo’s treatment of projectile motion and the superposition of horizontal uniform motion with vertical motion under gravity. It is a historical/conceptual example rather than a numerical exercise. The essential conclusion is that the ideal trajectory is parabolic because the horizontal displacement is proportional to time while vertical displacement includes a term proportional to time squared.

The source considers a hiker standing at the edge of a cliff and a stone/projectile launched horizontally or obliquely, using the independent horizontal and vertical equations of projectile motion. The coordinate origin is chosen at the cliff edge, x positive along the initial horizontal direction and y positive upward. Vertical motion is governed by gravity. content.text: Uniform circular motion occurs when an object moves along a circular path at constant speed. Its velocity changes continuously in direction and is tangent to the circle, so the object is accelerated even though its speed is constant. The acceleration points toward the centre and is called centripetal acceleration. Its magnitude is ac = v²/R. The magnitude is constant for constant speed and radius, but the acceleration vector is not constant because its direction changes continuously. The chapter notes the historical contribution of Christiaan Huygens, whose analysis of centripetal acceleration was published in 1673, and attributes the term “centripetal” to Newton.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Uniform circular motion and centripetal acceleration

content.text: Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angular displacement, ω = Δθ/Δt. For motion on a circle of radius R, arc length satisfies Δs = RΔθ, so linear speed v = Rω. The time for one revolution is the period T, and the number of revolutions per second is frequency ν = 1/T. Therefore ω = 2πν, v = 2πR/T = 2πRν, and ac = ω²R = 4π²ν²R.

metadata.topic: Angular speed, period and frequency in circular motion

content.text: Problem: An insect moves steadily in a circular groove of radius 12 cm and completes 7 revolutions in 100 s. The angular speed is ω = 2π(7/100) ≈ 0.44 rad s⁻¹. Linear speed is v = ωR = 0.44 s⁻¹ × 12 cm ≈ 5.3 cm s⁻¹. The velocity is tangent to the circle and acceleration is directed toward the centre. The acceleration vector is not constant because its direction changes, but its magnitude is constant: a = ω²R = (0.44 s⁻¹)²(12 cm) ≈ 2.3 cm s⁻².

content.text: The chapter summary states that scalars have magnitude only, whereas vectors have magnitude and direction. A vector multiplied by λ changes magnitude by |λ| and reverses direction if λ is negative. Vectors may be added by triangle or parallelogram methods; addition is commutative and associative. A zero vector has zero magnitude. Subtraction is addition of the negative vector. A vector can be resolved into components along independent directions, and Cartesian components make analytical addition straightforward.

The position vector in the x-y plane is r = xi + yj and displacement is Δr = r′ − r. Average velocity is Δr/Δt and instantaneous velocity is dr/dt, tangent to the trajectory. Average acceleration is Δv/Δt and instantaneous acceleration is dv/dt. For constant acceleration, v = v₀ + at and r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at². Ideal projectile motion is the superposition of horizontal uniform motion and vertical acceleration −g; its path is parabolic, with standard formulas for maximum height, time to peak and range.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Chapter summary: velocity, acceleration and projectile motion

content.text: In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant but velocity changes direction. Centripetal acceleration has magnitude ac = v²/R and points toward the centre. Angular speed relates to linear speed through v = ωR. With period T and frequency ν, ω = 2πν, v = 2πRν and ac = 4π²ν²R.

The path length between two points generally differs from the magnitude of displacement. Displacement depends only on endpoints, while path length depends on the route. They are equal only if the object does not change direction. Consequently, average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity; equality holds when path length equals displacement magnitude.

content.text: The vector equations for constant acceleration do not depend on a particular coordinate system, though components may be resolved along chosen axes. Constant-acceleration kinematic equations do not apply directly to uniform circular motion because the acceleration direction changes. For two objects with velocities v₁ and v₂ measured in the same reference frame, the resultant of velocities applied to an object is distinct from relative velocity: v₁₂ = v₁ − v₂. In circular motion, acceleration points toward the centre only when speed is constant. Trajectory depends on acceleration and initial conditions, including initial position and velocity.
